nameStory: The name 'lady's-mantle' comes from the plant's distinctive leaves, which were thought to resemble the flowing cloak or mantle worn by medieval ladies. The genus name Alchemilla has an even more magical origin - medieval alchemists believed the perfect water droplets that collected on these leaves were the purest form of water, essential for their quest to turn base metals into gold!
description: Garden lady's-mantle is a low-growing perennial herb that forms attractive clumps about 12-18 inches tall and wide. Its most striking feature is its soft, rounded leaves that look like pleated fans with scalloped edges. The plant produces sprays of tiny chartreuse-yellow flowers that seem to float above the foliage like delicate clouds. Originally from Southern Europe, it's now a popular garden plant that can spread freely by self-seeding.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive fan-shaped leaves with 7-11 shallow lobes and scalloped, toothed edges. Feel soft and velvety due to fine hairs, especially on the undersides. The leaves have prominent radiating veins like the ribs of an umbrella.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Masses of tiny chartreuse or yellow-green flowers without petals, each about 1/8 inch across, held in loose, airy clusters above the leaves. Individual flowers have 4 sepals and look like miniature green stars.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, rounded clumps that spread slowly outward. Leaves emerge directly from the ground on long stalks, creating a mounded appearance like a soft green cushion.

idTips.label: Water Beading
idTips.description: After rain or in morning dew, water forms perfect spherical droplets on the leaves rather than soaking in, creating a magical jeweled appearance that's unmistakable.

habitat: Garden lady's-mantle is primarily found in cultivated settings like perennial gardens, rock gardens, and landscaped areas throughout New England. It occasionally escapes cultivation and can be found naturalized in disturbed soils, woodland edges, and along roadsides. Prefers rich, moist, well-drained soil and partial shade but tolerates full sun in cooler locations.

seasonality.spring: Fresh leaves emerge in early spring, unfurling with a distinctive pleated appearance. Young leaves are especially soft and silvery-green with prominent water-beading properties.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from late spring through mid-summer, with chartreuse flower clusters rising 6-12 inches above the foliage. Leaves remain lush and green if given adequate moisture.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow-brown after hard frosts but often persist well into fall. Seeds ripen and scatter, potentially creating new plants nearby.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh winters, though in protected spots some basal leaves may persist. Crown remains alive underground, ready to sprout again in spring.

funFact: The water droplets that form on lady's-mantle leaves are so perfectly spherical that they look like liquid mercury! This happens because the leaves have a special waxy coating that repels water - the same principle used in modern waterproof fabrics, but perfected by nature millions of years ago.
confusionNotes: The fan-shaped, lobed leaves might remind you of wild geraniums or some maple seedlings, but lady's-mantle's leaves are much softer to the touch and have that distinctive scalloped edge all around. The tiny chartreuse flowers in airy clusters are also completely different from anything else you'll see.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this garden species with native lady's-mantles or the alpine lady's-mantle that was actually used medicinally - garden lady's-mantle has no traditional medicinal history despite what some sources claim. It's considered invasive in some regions because it self-seeds so readily, so check local guidelines before planting.
compareHints: Garden lady's-mantle is much larger and more robust than its relatives like slender parsley-piert, which has tiny divided leaves and grows as a small annual weed. The other lady's-mantles in our region are much smaller plants with more deeply divided leaves and lack the soft, velvety texture of garden lady's-mantle's generous foliage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Slender parsley-piert differs dramatically from its showy cousin Garden Lady's-mantle, which has large, soft leaves and grows over a foot tall.
Velvet Lady's-mantle is distinguished from other Lady's-mantles by its exceptionally hairy, truly velvety texture throughout.
Thin-stem Lady's-mantle is distinguished from Garden Lady's-mantle by its much more delicate build and notably slender stems.
